newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Foreigners get more chance in Russian market.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Foreigners get more chance in Russian market.

text.p: Russia, long a difficult place for Westerners to do business, has promised foreigners equal access to its lucrative government debt markets by the end of this year, a senior central bank official said on Friday.

Non-residents, who were only allowed to officially trade government securities in Russia early last year, will be treated just like Russians, central bank First Deputy Chairman Sergei Aleksashenko told Reuters Financial Television.

"Russia has agreed with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) generally that by the end of 1997 non-residents will receive the full rights which Russian participants in the government securities market now have," he said.
"An important element of our policy is the long-term liberalisation of non-resident participation in the government securities market."
Russian government securities have been offering some of the highest real interest rates in the world, but curbs on who can play the market mean the best returns are reserved for Russians.
Treasury bill yields are currently above 30 percent, with inflation expected to be about 12 percent this year.
Rates peaked at almost 190 percent in May of last year, just before the poll that re-elected President Boris Yeltsin.
Currently Westerners are forced to buy treasury bills and government bonds through special "S" accounts at government-approved banks. They receive a guaranteed dollar yield, currently 12.5 percent.
Profits can only be repatriated under certain conditions because the central bank is anxious to avoid a destabilising sudden outflow of funds.
Dealers say some foreigners have ignored government rules, however, and traded through Russian allies and partners.
Aleksashenko said the envisioned liberalisation would occur in stages. Officials say this is needed to prevent their boom market from suddenly going bust.
He said tight monetary policies had brought inflation down to 22 percent last year. Consumer prices rose almost 1,000 percent in 1993.

He also said the bank and the Federal Securities Commission, which governs Russia's securities markets, had patched up recent public disputes and agreed an ideological framework to develop the Russian market.
"By the end of 1998, Russia will enter the company of countries with acknowledged stable markets," he said.
The Russian markets offer a high-yield, high-risk ride for outside investors, and foreigners led a rally which has pushed the domestic share market up some 30 percent in the last month.

The equities market is much less restrictive than the market for government securities and the IMF, which has blessed Russian economic reforms with a three-year $10 billion loan, has put pressure on the authorities to eliminate bond market curbs.
